Eaton's brook mayfly (Habrophlebia lauta) is a small leptophlebiid found in the clear, cool headwater streams of the western Palearctic, with a univoltine life cycle completing one generation per year. The egg measures just 0.0211 centimeters  in length, a small dimension typical of mayflies that deposit their eggs directly onto the streambed. Under an assumed water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the age at birth is approximately 18 days [ab = approximately 18 days], after which the newly hatched larva emerges at a total length at hatching of just 0.01 centimeters [Lb = 0.01 centimeters].

Following hatching, the aquatic nymph undergoes a prolonged period of growth within the streambed, grazing on periphyton and fine particulate organic matter accumulated among the gravel and leaf litter. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at emergence reaches approximately 363 days , reflecting nearly a full year of larval development that underlies the species' univoltine life history. Over the course of this extended larval phase, the nymph grows to an ultimate larval length of 0.75 centimeters , accumulating a maximum dry weight of nymph of approximately 0.00102 grams .

Upon completing larval development, the nymph emerges from the water as a winged subimago and subsequently molts into the reproductively mature imago, attaining an ultimate forewing length of 0.8 centimeters [Li = 0.8 centimeters]. This adult stage is remarkably brief: at the same reference temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the life span as (sub)adult is only about 2 days [am = about 2 days], a hallmark of mayflies, whose non-feeding winged stages exist solely to disperse, mate, and oviposit before dying. This extremely compressed adult phase, following nearly a year of larval growth, completes the univoltine annual cycle characteristic of the species.

Reproductive investment in Eaton's brook mayfly is concentrated entirely within this brief adult window. Under a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], females carry a total number of eggs of approximately 790 , all of which are deposited in a single reproductive bout before the adult perishes. This strategy of a single, large egg batch produced during an extremely short adult lifespan is a common pattern among mayflies, which forgo any adult feeding in favor of rapid reproduction immediately following emergence, ensuring that the entire life-history investment culminates in a synchronized pulse of oviposition into the natal stream.
